cards.headline: Compound interest: growth on growth
lines: When interest is added to the balance, the next round of interest is paid on it too.
At 7% a year, an amount roughly doubles in about 10 years.
Time matters as much as the rate: the longer it runs, the steeper the curve.
cards.source: The compound-interest formula A = P(1 + r)^t, as in any introductory finance text.

cards.headline: The Rule of 72
lines: Divide 72 by a yearly growth rate to estimate how many years it takes to double.
At 6% that's about 12 years; at 9%, about 8.
It works for debt too: an unpaid balance at 24% a year can double in about 3 years.
cards.source: The Rule of 72, a standard approximation in introductory finance texts.

cards.headline: Inflation shrinks what money buys
lines: When prices rise across the economy, each unit of money buys a little less.
At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years (72 ÷ 3).
A 'real' return is the headline rate minus inflation.
cards.source: Mankiw, 'Principles of Economics', chapters on inflation.

cards.headline: Not every egg in one basket
lines: Diversification spreads money across many investments, so one failure hurts less.
It reduces the risk tied to a single company — but not the ups and downs of the whole market.
cards.source: Markowitz (1952), 'Portfolio Selection', Journal of Finance; Bodie, Kane & Marcus, 'Investments'.

cards.headline: Opportunity cost: the road not taken
lines: Every choice costs the best alternative you give up.
Time has an opportunity cost too: an hour on one thing is an hour not spent on another.
Comparing options, not just prices, leads to better decisions.
cards.source: Mankiw, 'Principles of Economics', the Ten Principles of Economics.

cards.question: You put 100 in an account paying 10% a year, compounded yearly. How much is there after 2 years?
cards.why: Year 1: 100 becomes 110. Year 2: 10% of 110 is 11, so 121. The extra 1 is interest on interest.

cards.question: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 8% a year?
cards.why: 72 ÷ 8 = 9. It's an approximation, but a close one at everyday rates.
cards.source: The Rule of 72, introductory finance texts.

cards.question: Savings earn 2% a year while prices rise 4% a year. What happens to what the savings can buy?
cards.why: The real return is roughly 2% − 4% = −2%: the number grows, but its buying power falls.
cards.source: Mankiw, 'Principles of Economics', real and nominal interest rates.

cards.question: A product suddenly becomes scarce while demand stays the same. Its price usually…
cards.why: Supply and demand: less supply with unchanged demand pushes the price up.
cards.source: Mankiw, 'Principles of Economics', supply and demand.

cards.question: What does diversification mainly reduce?
cards.why: Spreading out cuts company-specific risk. Market-wide swings remain.

cards.headline: The first coins came from Lydia
cards.text: Around the 7th century BCE, the kingdom of Lydia, in today's western Turkey, struck coins from electrum, a natural gold–silver alloy.
cards.source: Davies, 'A History of Money from Ancient Times to the Present Day'.

cards.headline: China used paper money a thousand years ago
cards.text: Song-dynasty China issued government paper notes in the 11th century, centuries before paper money was common in Europe.
cards.source: Davies, 'A History of Money'; von Glahn, 'Fountain of Fortune' (1996).

cards.headline: Central banks raise rates to cool inflation
cards.text: Higher interest rates make borrowing costlier, which slows spending and, with a delay, slows price rises.

cards.headline: Gresham's law: bad money drives out good
cards.text: When two coins have the same face value but different metal content, people hoard the better one and spend the worse.
cards.source: Named after Sir Thomas Gresham (16th century); standard economic history texts.

cards.headline: How a market price forms

steps.headline: 1 · Demand
lines: Demand is how much people want to buy at each price.
Usually, as the price falls, people buy more.

steps.headline: 2 · Supply
lines: Supply is how much sellers offer at each price.
Usually, a higher price brings more supply, because producing pays better.

steps.headline: 3 · Equilibrium
lines: The price settles where the amount wanted meets the amount offered.
Above it, unsold goods pile up; below it, shortages appear.

steps.headline: 4 · Shifts
lines: When demand or supply shifts, the price moves.
A bad harvest cuts supply and raises prices; a new craze raises demand and prices.

cards.source: Mankiw, 'Principles of Economics', the market forces of supply and demand.

cards.headline: Money: the takeaways
points: Every choice has an opportunity cost.
